title: Context Engineering & Guardrails
tagline: Write the constraint file that keeps an AI agent inside scope during real build work.
intro: When an engineer runs an AI coding agent at Level 3 (agentic, with approval checkpoints) or Level 4 (more autonomous), the agent doesn't work off tribal knowledge — it works off whatever's written down. That written-down file is where a PM's judgment gets encoded, and increasingly, PMs are the ones best positioned to write it. The same pattern applies whether the agent is touching I-9 review, ACA reporting, or any other regulated Employer Services workflow: the constraints are a product decision before they're an engineering one.

scenario.context: Engineering is ready to build the I-9 Completion Assistant using an AI coding agent running at Level 3 (it can write and test code across multiple files, but a human approves before anything merges).
scenario.brief: Before the engineering team starts the agent, they've asked you — the PM — to write the guardrail file that will sit alongside the code and constrain what the agent is allowed to do. This is the file the agent reads before it takes any action.

sections.heading: Project context
sections.learning: What is this system, in plain terms, with no assumed prior knowledge? Level 1 is autocomplete, Level 2 is chat-assist, Level 3 is agentic-with-approval, Level 4 is autonomous agentic — your role shifts at each level, from writing tickets to writing the bounds the agent operates inside. This section sets the stage for everything after it.

example.text: This service reviews I-9 forms and supporting documents for Meridian Logistics new hires against federal employment-eligibility requirements, and flags issues for HR admin review. It does not contact employees directly, and it does not make final approve/reject decisions — a human HR admin reviews every flag.

field.label: Your turn: Project context
field.help: What is this system, in plain terms, with no assumed prior knowledge?
field.placeholder: Describe the system as if the reader has never seen it.

sections.heading: Allowed actions
sections.learning: What's explicitly in scope for the agent to build or change? Forbidden actions and escalation rules are product judgment calls, not just technical ones — what's an acceptable risk, what needs a human in the loop. An engineer can write the technical constraints; a PM is often the right person to write the product ones.

example.text: Read I-9 form data and document images, compare against federal requirement rules, generate a list of flagged issues with citations, generate an internal note for the HR admin. Nothing else.

field.label: Your turn: Allowed actions
field.help: What's explicitly in scope for the agent to build or change?

sections.heading: Forbidden actions
sections.learning: What must the agent never do, even if it seems reasonable in the moment? This is the section worth the most care — a vague 'be careful' isn't a constraint an agent can act on; a specific prohibition is.

example.text: Never contact the new hire directly. Never mark an I-9 as approved or rejected — only flag or don't flag. Never state a federal requirement that isn't in the source rules document. Never store or output a document image alongside a person's full Social Security number in plain text.

field.label: Your turn: Forbidden actions
field.help: What must the agent never do, even if it seems reasonable in context?
field.placeholder: List the hard no's, as concretely as possible.

sections.heading: Escalation rules
sections.learning: What situations should stop the agent and require a human decision? This is the same discipline that governs any regulated Employer Services flow — an ACA reporting assistant, for instance, would need its own explicit escalation rule for anything touching a filing deadline.

example.text: Any document type the model hasn't been trained to recognize. Any new hire previously flagged in a compliance audit. Any case where required fields conflict between the I-9 and the supporting document in a way the rules don't clearly resolve.

field.label: Your turn: Escalation rules
field.help: What situations should stop the agent and require a human decision?
field.placeholder: List the trigger conditions for stopping and asking a human.

sections.heading: Definition of done
sections.learning: How would anyone — human or agent — know this work is actually finished and safe to ship?

example.text: Every flagged issue cites a specific federal requirement. All test cases from the historical Meridian I-9 set produce the same flag/no-flag outcome an HR admin already reached. No test case contains a fabricated requirement or a stored raw SSN.

field.label: Your turn: Definition of done
field.help: How would anyone know this work is actually finished and safe to ship?
